Verify an RFC 3161 timestamp token

Source: R/timestamp.R
tsvrf.Rd

A timestamp token is a small file, signed by an independent timestamping authority, saying that a given set of bytes (for example a manifest of results) existed at a given time. tsvrf() checks that a token covers the bytes given, reports the time it asserts, and verifies the timestamping authority's signature under a certificate you supply or the one the token carries. tsinfo() reads the token's fields without verifying anything. Use them to prove that an analysis output existed by a certain date.

Usage

tsvrf(token, data, cert = NULL, trust = NULL, crls = list(), attm = NULL)

tsinfo(token)

Arguments

token

The token: a raw vector, or a path to a .tsr / .tst file. A full TimeStampResp or a bare TimeStampToken are both accepted.

data

The bytes the token should cover: a raw vector, or a path to a file.

cert

The authority's certificate, DER or PEM, as raw or a path. Optional: when the token embeds a certificate, that one is used and the fact is reported.

trust

Trust anchors for validating that certificate – see certchnvrf(). Without them the signature is still checked, but nothing vouches for the key that made it.

crls

Optional CRLs to check the chain against, as raw vectors or paths.

attm

The time to check certificate validity at. Defaults to the time the token asserts, which is usually what is wanted.

Value

tsvrf() returns a list of class bricklayer_timestamp: ok (logical), time (a POSIXct in UTC, or NA when the token could not be read), serial and policy (character), hash_algorithm (for example "sha256"), signature_algorithm (an OID string), and a checks data frame with columns check, ok and detail. The print method lists the checks. tsinfo() returns a plain list with time, serial, policy, hash_algorithm, imprint (hex), signature_algorithm and has_certificate (logical).

Details

Every step is recorded as a row of checks:

  • token_parses;

  • token_structure;

  • message_imprint (the hash of data equals the token's imprint);

  • certificate_source;

  • signature;

  • attribute_digest (the signed attributes commit to the token's contents);

  • certificate_trust;

  • with trust, the chain: checks of certchnvrf().

ok is TRUE only when every row passes. A token that cannot be parsed is not an error: it gives ok = FALSE and the rows up to the failure.

Pass trust and the certificate is validated too: the chain is built to an anchor you name, every signature in it is verified, every validity window is checked, an issuer must be a CA, and the leaf must carry the timeStamping extended key usage. Omit trust and the signature is still checked but certificate_trust is reported as failed, because without an anchor a passing signature says only that the key in the certificate signed the token – not that anyone should believe that certificate.

Validity windows are checked at the time the TOKEN asserts, unless attm says otherwise. A token signed in 2020 under a certificate that expired in 2021 was validly signed, and judging it by today's date would reject it for a reason unconnected to its validity.

RSA and ECDSA over the NIST prime curves P-256, P-384 and P-521 are verified. Anything else – a post-quantum signature, a compressed EC point, an Edwards curve – is reported as unverifiable rather than treated as valid, which is the safe direction for a verifier.

Revocation data are not fetched: a CRL has to be handed in through crls, and nothing is retrieved over the network (chain checks such as name constraints and certificate policies are done by certchnvrf()). Nothing is written to disk.

Errors: token, data or cert neither a raw vector nor the path of an existing file. tsinfo() errors on a token it cannot parse.

References

Adams, C., Cain, P., Pinkas, D., and Zuccherato, R. (2001). Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure Time-Stamp Protocol (TSP). RFC 3161.

See also

chnseal() for the ordering a timestamp cannot give, cpsatst() for authorship.

Examples

# Offline: bytes that are not a timestamp token are reported, not
# thrown, so a batch check can carry on.
bad <- tsvrf(as.raw(c(0x30, 0x03, 0x02, 0x01, 0x05)),
                        data = charToRaw("manifest"))
bad$ok
#> [1] FALSE
bad$checks
#>             check    ok                         detail
#> 1    token_parses  TRUE                 5 bytes of DER
#> 2 token_structure FALSE no CMS SignedData in the token

# tsinfo() does refuse an unreadable token
try(tsinfo(as.raw(1:10)))
#> Error : trailing bytes after the DER structure: 4 of 10 consumed

# Real tokens come from a timestamping authority; this is the shape of
# the call.
if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
res <- tsvrf("response.tsr", data = "manifest.json")
res$ok
res$time
} # }
